 Waymo Files 2 Recalls: Closed Freeway Lanes, Hand Signals
 Daniel Roth 
 Updated Nov 21, 2026 · 15 min read 
 Image: Alphabet Waymo told federal regulators it is recalling its robotaxi software twice over, once for closed freeway lanes and once for intersections where police or emergency crews direct traffic by hand. Reuters reported the two filings on Friday, November 20, 2026, saying Alphabet’s self-driving unit filed both with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) the day before. The Waymo recall covers the company’s 5th Generation Automated Driving System, and it lands days after Waymo pulled its cars off US freeways entirely.

 Related Coverage 
 The timing matters as much as the content. California’s Department of Motor Vehicles had already barred driverless Waymo cars from state freeways, a ban we covered in our report on Waymo being barred from all California freeways since November 11 . The new recalls give that standoff a federal paper trail, and they raise a question the company has not yet answered in public: when does the fix for closed freeway lanes ship?
 This analysis walks through what Waymo filed, what remains unconfirmed, how the filings connect to a 3,871-system recall from earlier this year, and what the episode says about the hardware fleet that robotaxi operators now run at scale. It also compares Waymo’s position with rivals and closes with five predictions, clearly labeled as our own analysis.

 Add now What Waymo Filed With NHTSA in the Waymo Recall
 Waymo filed two separate safety recalls. Reuters, citing a Waymo statement, said both target the company’s automated driving system and aim, in Waymo’s words, “to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control.” That is the only direct quotation from the company in the coverage we reviewed, so everything else in this piece paraphrases.
 The first filing deals with a failure mode in which a Waymo vehicle may enter a closed freeway lane and keep driving in it. The second deals with how a vehicle responds to manual commands from law enforcement or emergency personnel at intersections. Waymo reported no collisions or injuries from the closed-freeway events. The manual-control filing is different. Reuters said it follows a collision in which a Waymo obeyed an officer’s directions, after which the officer became temporarily obstructed.

 Several details are still missing. The reports do not give the number of vehicles covered by the two November filings, and they do not list the NHTSA recall identification numbers. They also say nothing about per-vehicle repair costs. We will not guess at any of those figures here.
 The Closed Freeway Lane Recall, Explained
 A closed freeway lane looks simple to a human driver. Cones taper across the lane, an arrow board flashes, and the traffic ahead merges away. For software, the same scene is a puzzle of partial evidence. Cones may be sparse, signs may sit far upstream, and other cars may still be driving where a human would expect nobody to be.
 What the filing says
 Waymo described the problem as unusual circumstances in which a vehicle may enter and continue driving in a closed freeway lane. The company said it is still developing the remedy. That detail deserves attention. A recall with a finished remedy tells owners and regulators the problem is contained. A recall with an unfinished remedy tells them the company has named the problem but has not yet solved it.
 What stays open
 Waymo has not given a ship date for the closed-lane fix. It also has not said whether the fix will be validated on public freeways with safety drivers, in simulation, or both. Wired reported that Waymo will keep testing on highways with safety operators behind the wheel while commercial freeway rides stay off. That suggests the validation path runs through supervised driving, though the company has not spelled it out.
 The Manual Traffic Control Recall
 Manual traffic control is the messy human layer on top of a rules-based road. An officer waves cars through a dead signal. A crossing guard holds up a hand. A firefighter points a flashlight at a lane. People read these cues in half a second, and they know an officer’s instruction can override a green light.
 Waymo said the recall addresses how its vehicles respond to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or emergency personnel. The trigger, per Reuters, was a collision in which a Waymo followed an officer’s directions and the officer was then temporarily obstructed. The reports do not say who was hurt, where it happened, or what the obstruction was, and we will not fill those gaps.
 One fact stands out. Waymo said the software update for this recall was completed on November 6, 2026. That is two weeks before the public announcement. So the manual-control recall is a paperwork catch-up on a fix already on the road, while the closed-lane recall is an open problem. The two filings carry very different risk profiles even though they share a headline.
 For fleet operators, the lesson is about priority rules. When an officer’s signal conflicts with a traffic light, the car has to know which instruction wins, and it has to keep honoring that instruction when the officer steps out of view. Waymo’s description of the officer being temporarily obstructed hints that the system’s handling of a signal that disappears mid-maneuver was part of the problem, though the company has not said so directly.
 Timeline: From Cones in Phoenix to Two New Recalls
 The new filings are the latest step in a sequence that started in the spring. The table below stitches together dates from NHTSA’s recall report, Reuters, and Wired. Rows marked as reported come from press accounts of the filings rather than from the filings themselves.
 Date Event Source basis 
 April 2026 Waymo cars reportedly drove past ramp closure signs into planned freeway construction in Phoenix Reported, citing the federal filing 
 May 18, 2026 Seven Waymo vehicles entered active freeway construction lanes in the San Francisco Bay Area NHTSA recall report 
 May 19, 2026 Waymo’s Field Safety Committee met on the events NHTSA recall report 
 June 16, 2026 Waymo began updating affected software NHTSA recall report 
 June 25, 2026 Freeway operations began resuming NHTSA recall report 
 November 6, 2026 Manual traffic control update completed Reuters, citing Waymo 
 November 11, 2026 California DMV freeway ban took effect Wired, citing the DMV 
 November 19, 2026 Two recalls filed with NHTSA Reuters 
 November 20, 2026 Recalls announced publicly Reuters 
 Read top to bottom, the table shows a gap of about five months between the first freeway recall and the second wave. In between, freeway service resumed, and Waymo’s fix for construction zones went into the fleet. The new closed-lane recall suggests that fix did not cover every shape a closed lane can take.
 The 3,871-System Precedent
 The earlier recall, campaign 26E035, is the benchmark. NHTSA’s recall report identifies 3,871 affected systems. It says seven Waymo autonomous vehicles entered freeway lanes with active construction in the Bay Area on May 18, 2026, by driving between cones that marked a lane closure.
 Waymo began updating the affected software on June 16, 2026 and started resuming freeway operations on June 25. The remedy was meant to improve recognition of freeway construction zones, rank them above other freeway hazards, and cut speed when a zone might be present. That last element matters. Slowing down when unsure is a conservative design choice, and it trades travel time for margin.
 The Register covered the June recall under a headline about robotaxis that keep missing the signs for freeway construction zones . The word “keep” proved prescient. Five months later, the company is back with a second freeway recall, and the reporting does not tie the new filing to a specific new crash.
 The detail worth underlining is the speed rule. Reducing speed when a construction zone might be detected means the car treats uncertainty as a reason to slow, not as a reason to carry on. If the new closed-lane remedy follows the same logic, riders could see more cautious freeway behavior when Waymo returns to the road. Waymo has not described the design of the new remedy, so that remains our inference.
 California’s Ban and the Nationwide Freeway Pause
 The recalls did not arrive in a vacuum. Wired reported that the California DMV barred Waymo’s vehicles from state freeway operations beginning November 11, after the department concluded that Waymo’s freeway driving posed an imminent hazard to public safety. Waymo then stopped highway driving in all of its markets.
 A DMV spokesperson pointed to two incidents. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. In the other, a viral video showed a Waymo interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as officers tried to enforce a traffic break while workers cleared crash debris. The DMV said the ban stays until Waymo proves it has taken effective corrective actions. Patch also covered the ban in its Los Angeles edition.

 Readers tracking the standoff can compare our earlier pieces. One looked at what California wants from Waymo, three proofs and no restore dates . Another covered Waymo pausing freeway rides in five markets, Austin included . The new recalls plug directly into that story, because a federal remedy filing is the kind of corrective action the DMV says it needs to see.
 Surface-street service continues. Wired said Waymo still runs in 15 metros, including parts of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.
 The Hardware Angle: A Software Fix on a Sensor Fleet
 This story belongs in the hardware conversation because a robotaxi is a rolling sensor and compute platform, and the 5th Generation system named in the filings is the hardware-software stack that sits on each car. The recall language centers on the automated driving system. The reporting we reviewed describes updates and remedies, not part replacements, and Waymo has not said any sensor or compute change is involved.
 Why software recalls still matter for hardware buyers
 A fleet operator that can push a software update overnight has a cost edge over a carmaker that must bring cars to a dealer. It also carries a risk the old model did not. A patch that does not hold, and then needs a second recall, drains trust faster than a one-time dealer fix would. Wired noted that NHTSA is separately examining whether another earlier Waymo software fix actually solved its robotaxis’ problems.
 What to watch in the fleet
 Reuters ran a photo of a Zeekr-built Waymo vehicle charging in San Diego on August 19, 2026, which shows the fleet now includes a vehicle made by the Chinese automaker Zeekr. Whether the recalls touch that platform is unconfirmed. Buyers of autonomous hardware, and investors who track it, should watch for any filing that names specific vehicle models, because that would show where the fix has to land.
 There is also a data question hiding in the hardware story. Every recall like this depends on the operator’s logs, the sensor records that show what the car perceived and why it chose to proceed. Regulators will lean on those records to judge whether a remedy works. How much of that evidence Waymo shares with NHTSA and the DMV will shape how fast trust returns.
 The Regulatory Pile-Up Around Waymo
 The two freeway and intersection recalls are not the only federal file open on Waymo. Reuters wrote that NHTSA opened a recall query last week into Waymo vehicles after numerous incidents of robotaxis passing stopped school buses. That probe covers nearly 3,000 company-owned self-driving vehicles, and investigators want to know whether a software update rolled out late last year failed to stop the problem. Most of the violations happened after Waymo said the remedy had been deployed.
 Reuters added that NHTSA and the National Transportation Safety Board opened separate probes after a Waymo struck a child in January near an elementary school in Santa Monica, California. The table below lines up the open items using only what the reports state.
 Issue Status per reports Scale stated Remedy status 
 Closed freeway lanes (Nov. 2026 recall) Filed with NHTSA, no collisions or injuries reported Vehicle count unconfirmed Still being developed 
 Manual traffic control (Nov. 2026 recall) Filed with NHTSA, follows one collision Vehicle count unconfirmed Update completed Nov. 6 
 Freeway construction (26E035) Recall issued, freeway ops resumed June 25 3,871 systems, 7 vehicles on May 18 Update began June 16 
 School bus passing NHTSA recall query opened Nearly 3,000 company-owned vehicles Under review by NHTSA 
 Santa Monica child strike (January) NHTSA and NTSB probes opened 1 incident Not applicable 
 Waymo’s counterpoint, stated in Reuters, is that its technology outperforms statistically comparable human benchmarks and sharply reduces injury-causing crashes. Regulators have not publicly weighed that claim against the recall record in the coverage we found. The tension between the safety statistics and the recall count is the core of the policy fight.
 Market Impact for Alphabet and the Robotaxi Sector
 Waymo is a unit of Alphabet, and none of the reports we reviewed cite a stock move or a revenue impact tied to the recalls. We will not invent one. What the filings do change is the product mix. Freeway rides were a service Waymo only began offering last year, and they are now off across the network.
 With freeway service off across the whole network, Waymo’s reachable trip map shrinks to surface streets in its 15 metros. The company said it is working with California and other state officials to resume freeway operations. A staged return, state by state, looks more plausible than a single switch, and in California the DMV controls the pace.

 Local governments are watching too. Our report on Denver wanting to regulate Waymo’s 60 cars while state law blocks it shows how patchy city and state oversight of robotaxis remains. A federal recall record gives local officials something concrete to point at, even where they lack the power to act on it.
 How Waymo Compares With Rivals
 Waymo is the benchmark operator, so its recalls shape how regulators view everyone else. The comparison below uses only figures we can source. Where reporting gives no number, the cell says so.
 Operator Fleet or footprint cited Construction or hand-signal record in our sources 
 Waymo 15 metros, nearly 3,000 company-owned vehicles in the school bus probe Two Nov. 2026 recalls, 3,871-system recall earlier 
 Pony AI 2,768 robotaxis in Q3, per our earlier report Not covered in these filings 
 Tesla No current fleet figure in our sources Hand-signal handling covered in our Texas report 
 Zoox No current fleet figure in our sources Not covered in these filings 
 Our piece on Pony AI’s 2,768 robotaxis framing Tesla’s fleet question shows how scale claims travel across the industry. On the behavior side, we reported on a Tesla robotaxi that obeys hand signals in a Texas construction zone with no driver aboard . Those two behaviors, reading hand signals and handling work zones, are exactly what Waymo’s new recalls target.
 The takeaway for rivals is uncomfortable. If the market leader still needs two recalls on these skills, challengers with less road time should expect the same questions from regulators. Nothing in the filings says any rival has failed. They say the bar is higher than a clean demo.
 Historical Context: A Decade of Construction-Zone Trouble
 Wired wrote that self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade. The reason is structural. Zones can look and be arranged differently depending on the work being done and where, and there are no hard-and-fast rules for how bollards, placards, and blinking arrows must appear. Humans generalize from a few cues, and software needs training examples for each variation.
 Freeways raise the stakes. At highway speeds, workers share space with fast traffic, and a mistake leaves little time to recover. Waymo only began carrying passengers on freeways last year, according to Wired, so the company is still early in its freeway history. Its surface-street record spans far more miles and more years.
 Manual traffic control has its own history. An officer’s wave is rare for any single car, but a large fleet will meet it regularly. The recall follows a collision, and the update it describes was finished on November 6.
 What Remains Unconfirmed
 Careful readers should separate the confirmed from the open. Confirmed: the two filings, the problem descriptions, the absence of reported collisions or injuries in the closed-freeway events, the November 6 completion date for the manual-control update, and the 3,871-system earlier recall. Unconfirmed: the vehicle count in the new filings, the NHTSA recall numbers, any repair cost, and the vehicle models affected.
 Also unconfirmed is the link between the new closed-lane recall and the Route 101 event the DMV cited. The reports place them in the same news cycle, but they do not say the filing was written about that specific incident. Treat that connection as plausible, not established.
 Five Predictions for the Waymo Recall
 These are our own forecasts, not facts from the filings, and each could prove wrong.
 The closed-lane remedy will ship before California lifts its ban. The DMV wants proof of corrective action, and a finished remedy is the first piece of that proof.
 Freeway service will return in phases. Expect states without bans to restart sooner, with California last.
 NHTSA will keep widening its questions. With a school bus query and two freeway recalls open, a third request for data on any software remedy would not surprise us.
 Rivals will publish more about construction zones and hand signals. Operators that can show tested behavior will use it in pitches to regulators and city partners.
 Recall language will get more specific. Future filings will name vehicle counts and models earlier, since the first reports left those details blank.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What did Waymo recall?
 Waymo filed two safety recalls with NHTSA covering its 5th Generation Automated Driving System. One addresses vehicles that may enter and continue driving in a closed freeway lane. The other addresses responses to manual commands from police or emergency personnel at intersections.
 Were there any injuries?
 Waymo said no collisions or injuries were reported from the closed-freeway events. The manual-control recall follows a collision in which a Waymo followed an officer’s directions and the officer was then temporarily obstructed. Reports do not detail any injuries from that collision.
 Is the fix ready?
 Only partly. Waymo said the manual traffic control update was completed on November 6, 2026. It said the remedy for the closed freeway lane problem is still being developed.
 How many vehicles are affected?
 The reports on the November filings do not give a vehicle count. The earlier freeway construction recall, 26E035, identifies 3,871 affected systems, according to NHTSA’s recall report.
 Can I still ride a Waymo on the freeway?
 No, not for now. Wired reported that Waymo stopped highway driving in all of its markets after California’s DMV banned its vehicles from state freeways on November 11. Surface-street rides continue in the company’s 15 metros, and freeway testing continues with safety operators.
 Is this the first Waymo freeway recall?
 No. A June recall, campaign 26E035, covered freeway construction zones after seven vehicles entered active construction lanes in the Bay Area on May 18, 2026. Freeway operations began resuming on June 25.
 Does the recall affect other robotaxi companies?
 The filings name only Waymo. The practical effect on rivals is indirect, because regulators will likely ask other operators how their systems handle closed lanes and hand signals.
